item.title: New LSRP*-LA Planner Solves Large-Agent MAPF with Scalable Asynchronous Coordination
item.description:
New LSRP*-LA Planner Solves Large-Agent MAPF with Scalable Asynchronous Coordination

Researchers have introduced LSRP*-LA, a novel multi-agent path finding (MAPF) planner designed for large agents with asynchronous actions. Unlike prior approaches, LSRP*-LA scales to 800 agents, improves solution quality over time, and delivers near-optimal results for complex scenarios involving agents that occupy multiple cells.

📌 Overview

Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) aims to calculate collision-free paths for multiple agents moving from start to goal locations while minimizing total path costs. Traditional MAPF methods assume:

  • Each agent occupies a single vertex
  • All agents act synchronously

These constraints limit real-world applicability. Existing planners that relax both assumptions either struggle with scalability or fail to refine solutions effectively.

🧩 What’s New

The newly proposed LSRP*-LA addresses these limitations by supporting:

  • Large agents that occupy multiple cells
  • Asynchronous actions among agents

It builds upon LSRP*, a prior scalable and anytime planner with asynchronous capabilities, extending it to handle spatially larger agents.

⚙️ Key Details

Feature Description
Scalability Handles up to 800 agents on diverse maps
Anytime Improvement Continues enhancing solution quality post-initial output
Path Cost Efficiency Achieves roughly half the cost of synchronous planners for large agents
Agent Size Support Designed specifically for agents occupying multiple cells

🚀 Availability

The paper titled “LSRP-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions”* was submitted on 25 Nov 2026. A PDF and experimental HTML version are available online.

💡 Why It Matters

LSRP*-LA represents a significant advancement in robotics planning by overcoming two major limitations in existing MAPF algorithms. Its ability to scale efficiently while improving paths over time makes it especially valuable for deployments involving numerous spatially complex agents.

#multi-agentpathfinding #roboticsplanning #asynchronousagents #pathfindingalgorithm #scalableAI

Source: LSRP*-LA: Scalable and Anytime Multi-Agent Path Finding for Large Agents with Asynchronous Actions

item.title: New Python Package partialid Enables Tractable Sharp Bounds for Causal Inference with Unobserved Confounding
item.description:
New Python Package partialid Enables Tractable Sharp Bounds for Causal Inference with Unobserved Confounding

📚 Introduction

A new paper titled A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds (submitted 25 Nov 2026) presents a graphical criterion for deriving sharp causal bounds in the presence of unobserved confounding. The work introduces partialid, a Python package that enables users to compute sharp bounds efficiently using linear programming.

🧩 How it Works

The paper addresses the challenge of identifying causal effects and counterfactuals from observational data when unobserved confounding is present. Key contributions include:

  • Sharp bounds can be derived by solving one linear program when variables are discretely-valued and certain conditions hold.
  • For diagrams where each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, the paper provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to be optimal for any positive input probability table.

⚙️ Key Details

The approach is computationally tractable for many causal questions. The algorithm is implemented in the partialid Python package, which allows users to compose assumptions, queries, and data to obtain sharp bounds.

Component Description
partialid Python package for computing sharp causal bounds
Linear Programming Method used to derive sharp bounds under discrete variables
Graphical Criterion Determines when sharp bounds equal linear program optima

🚀 Availability

The paper is available on arXiv under the stat.ML category. The partialid package is listed in the associated code and data section, with tools like Hugging Face, DagsHub, and alphaXiv providing access to related resources.

💡 Why It Matters

This development advances causal inference methods by making sharp bound computation more accessible and efficient through a user-friendly software tool, particularly for scenarios with limited hidden confounders.

#CausalInference #MachineLearning #Python #Statistics #LinearProgramming

Source: A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds

item.title: Ellipsoid-Regularized Leverage Scores Enable Efficient Constrained Linear Regression
item.description:
Ellipsoid-Regularized Leverage Scores Enable Efficient Constrained Linear Regression

A new paper introduces ellipsoid‑regularized leverage scores for active learning in constrained linear regression, achieving lower query complexity while respecting constraint geometry.

🔍 Overview

  • The task: given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, find an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}|Ax-b|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible.
  • Conventional leverage‑score sampling ignores $C$ or encodes it with ridge regularization, leading to unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraints.

🧩 How it works

  • The authors approximate $C$ by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry.
  • This yields ellipsoid‑regularized leverage scores that adapt to the anisotropy of $C$.

⚙️ Key details

  • Query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$.
  • With appropriate parameters, $O\big(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2\big)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ whose objective value is at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times optimal.
  • For convex constraints, the dependence on $\varepsilon$ improves from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$.
  • Lower bounds show:
    • The $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence cannot be avoided without convexity assumptions on $C$.
    • For ellipsoidal constraints, a dependence of $d_{\text{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary in some regimes.

📊 Experiments

  • Synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem were used as testbeds.
  • The proposed method achieved lower regression error than standard baselines for a comparable query budget.

#activelearning #linearregression #leverageScores #optimization

Source: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression

item.title: New Counterexamples Challenge E-Means Clustering Algorithm
item.description:
New Counterexamples Challenge E-Means Clustering Algorithm

A new technical paper titled “Two Counterexamples for e-means” has been submitted, presenting cases where the e-means algorithm performs worse than standard k-means. The study focuses on the limitations of a method that combines exponential averaging and cluster revival.

🔍 Overview

The paper, submitted on November 17, 2026, by Zhenisbek Assylbekov, provides two counterexamples to the published recipe of e-means. These examples demonstrate that e-means can result in a higher final loss than the standard k-means algorithm (Lloyd, 1982) when starting from identical initial centers.

🧩 How it works

The analysis highlights specific failure modes of the e-means approach:

  • Mass-based revival: This component can destroy a global optimum.
  • Loss Ratio: The ratio of expected losses can become unbounded, even when using k-means++ seeding.

⚙️ Key details

  • Paper Title: Two Counterexamples for e-means
  • Submission Date: November 17, 2026
  • Author: Zhenisbek Assylbekov
  • Context: Computer Science > Machine Learning
  • Comparative Baseline: Standard k-means (Lloyd, 1982)

#MachineLearning #Clustering #kMeans #AlgorithmAnalysis

Source: Two Counterexamples for e-means

item.title: Goal-Branching LaCAM Improves Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
item.description:
Goal-Branching LaCAM Improves Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding

Goal-Branching LaCAM introduces temporary goals to help a multi‑agent pathfinding solver handle dense, corridor‑heavy environments.

🔍 Overview

  • LaCAM is a search‑based solver for Multi‑Agent Pathfinding (MAPF) that performs a depth‑first search over joint configurations.
  • It uses PIBT (Priority Inheritance with Backtracking) to generate successors and lazily adds single‑agent constraints to explore alternatives.
  • While complete, LaCAM struggles on dense maps because deadlocks often require coordinated moves of several agents away from their goals, which PIBT’s greedy one‑step successors rarely propose.

🧩 How Goal‑Branching Works

  • The paper proposes Goal‑Branching, where blocking agents receive temporary goals.
  • Each temporary goal is explored as an additional branch of LaCAM’s search.
  • Random and corridor‑aware rules are examined for selecting these temporary goals.
  • Completeness is preserved for any such rule.

⚙️ Key Results

Metric Goal‑Branching LaCAM LaCAM*
Solve rate on dense instances (60‑90% occupancy) 89% 44%
First‑solution speedup on maze‑32‑32‑2 and room‑32‑32‑4 (instances both solve) 10‑14× faster Baseline
Median time speedup at 75% density on room‑32‑32‑4 ~200× faster Baseline
Solution cost increase on instances both solve 15‑22% higher Baseline
Solution cost on open maps and full MovingAI benchmark No higher than LaCAM* (≤3% slower) Baseline

💡 Why It Matters

  • By adding temporary goals, the solver can break deadlocks without enumerating constraints agent by agent.
  • The approach retains the completeness of the original algorithm while dramatically improving success rates and runtime on challenging dense maps.
  • Cost overhead is modest and disappears on less congested environments.

Submitted on 5 Nov 2026

#MultiAgentPathfinding #AIPlanning #GoalBranching

Source: Goal-Branching LaCAM: Temporary Goals as Search Branches in Dense Multi-Agent Pathfinding
